newsitem.title: BOSNIA: NATO tells Moslem refugees -- Quit contested village.
newsitem.headline: NATO tells Moslem refugees -- Quit contested village.

text.p: NATO peacekeepers said on Wednesday they wanted Bosnian Moslem refugees reoccupying a devastated village on Serb territory to leave and apply for permission to return to their former homes.
A major dispute loomed after about 100 Moslems, some armed, entered Jusici, east of Tuzla, last Friday. They include pre-war residents of the village driven from their homes by fighting.

"The aim, as discussed in a number of meetings over the course of the past couple of days, was to see the settlers from Jusici move and get out of the area," NATO spokesman Major Brett Boudreau told reporters in Sarajevo.
Boudreau added that the goal was to get Bosnian Moslem and Serb authorities to agree to a six-point U.N. process governing a phased and orderly resettlement of villages such as Jusici.
Mostly destroyed in the 43-month Bosnian war, Jusici sits inside Serb-held territory and within a demilitarised "zone of separation" patrolled by NATO forces.
NATO troops seized and destroyed weapons from the Moslems and have urged Serb authorities not to enter the village.
International officials have sought since Friday to defuse the situation, with little apparent progress.
"I can tell you that nobody has a solution to this problem," a well-placed international official told Reuters on Wednesday, commenting on nearly a week of fruitless discussion.
Serb authorities insist that the Moslems withdraw and register to re-enter the village according to guidelines which were drawn up by the U.N. but have yet to be agreed by the parties.
U.N. officials said Bosnian Prime Minister Hasan Muratovic had agreed on Tuesday to pull the Moslems out of the village in exchange for speedy processing of their applications to return.
But Muratovic told reporters on Tuesday he was hoping the refugees would not have to leave the village and that the paperwork could, in effect, be completed retroactively.
U.N. sources also reported that the number of Moslems in the village had risen to 300. However Serb reports that some of them were digging trenches were disavowed by NATO.

"We understand that most of the people in the village are basically strictly rebuilding their homes, bringing in building supplies -- there's nothing sinister going on there," U.N. spokesman Alex Ivanko said.

Security in the area is being provided by a company of Russian paratroopers deployed in Bosnia as part of the NATO-led peace operation. Two U.N. police patrols are also operating regularly in the vicinity of Jusici.
Ivanko praised the professionalism of Serb police in the Jusici area and said they had not risen to the taunts of a group of young Moslems who tried to provoke an incident.
"One of the Moslems who returned, the former mayor, helped us get the young men out of the village and the Serbs performed with admirable restraint under the circumstances," Ivanko said.
